intro: Part I of The Rite of Spring, “Adoration of the Earth”, opens with a solo bassoon on a high C, and a few minutes later the strings play a repeated, stamping chord. Stravinsky conducts the Columbia Symphony Orchestra in this 1960 recording.

sections.label: Intro · Bassoon solo in high register
sections.mNote: A solo bassoon melody; other woodwinds enter in layers.

sections.label: A · Augurs of Spring
sections.mNote: Strings stamp; horns shift the accents.

sections.label: B · Ritual of Abduction
sections.mNote: Running strings and sharp wind cries.

sections.label: C · Spring Rounds, two clarinets, heavy dance
sections.mNote: Two clarinets play before the heavy dance begins.

sections.label: D · Ritual of the Rival Tribes
sections.mNote: Low brass set against quick, high figures.

sections.label: E · Procession of the Sage
sections.mNote: Tubas and horns play the procession theme.

sections.label: Link · The Sage kisses the earth
sections.mNote: Low winds, a quiet bass and held strings.

sections.label: F · Dance of the Earth
sections.mNote: Bass drum and rushing strings enter.

cues.title: Opening bassoon solo
cues.text: The bassoon opens alone, high in its range, with a short melody that turns around C. Other wind instruments then enter one by one, each with a phrase of its own.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 1–4, opening and rehearsal figures 1–4: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Letter to Nicholas Roerich, 1911
cues.text: Stravinsky wrote to the painter Nicholas Roerich on 26 September 1911, while composing the Augurs of Spring: “The picture of the old woman in a squirrel fur sticks in my mind.” He pictured her running before the dancers, stopping them and breaking into their rhythm.
cues.evidence: Stravinsky to Nicholas Roerich, 26 September 1911, on composing the Augurs of Spring; translated in Pieter C. van den Toorn, Stravinsky and The Rite of Spring (1987), pp. 3–4: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: Repeated chord with irregular accents
cues.text: The strings repeat a chord that combines F♭ major with an E♭ dominant seventh. Horns accent selected notes. The bars are written in 2/4, and the accents fall at irregular points within them.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 12–14, rehearsal figure 13: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, chapter 3, examples 15–18, analyses the chord and its accents in 2/4: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ritual of Abduction, opening
cues.text: Presto. The violins play running figures, the high winds play short bursts and the horns hold notes underneath. Each phrase is short, and the next one cuts it off.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 32–34, rehearsal figure 37 and the opening of the Ritual of Abduction: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E♭ and bass clarinets in octaves
cues.text: The E♭ clarinet and the bass clarinet play the same tune in octaves beneath trills in the flutes. The strings then enter, marked Sostenuto e pesante, with a heavy, even tread for the round dance.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 45–47, rehearsal figures 48–49, Tranquillo followed by Sostenuto e pesante: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Recording sessions, Brooklyn, 1960
cues.text: The orchestra recorded the work in the ballroom of Brooklyn’s St George Hotel on 5 and 6 January 1960, with the composer conducting. The music had first been heard with Nijinsky’s choreography for the ballet.
cues.evidence: Parnassus PACL 95003/4 booklet, p. 2, gives the performers, venue and session dates: https://media.musicalconcepts.net/wp-content/uploads/2021/06/28214506/PACL-95003_4-Booklet.pdf. Van den Toorn, pp. 1–6, describes the original ballet and Nijinsky’s choreography: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

cues.title: Two groups combined, figure 57
cues.text: Trombones and tubas play a heavy phrase. Faster figures follow in the upper register. Five bars into rehearsal figure 57 the two sound together, the low phrase continuing beneath the rapid upper parts.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 54–55, rehearsal figure 57: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, pp. 19–20, describes the two groups and their combination five bars into rehearsal figure 57: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Procession, tubas and horns
cues.text: The tubas repeat their tune while the horns play a different pattern. Bassoons and low strings keep moving underneath. The phrases are of unequal length, so the points where they coincide shift as the procession continues.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 65–73, rehearsal figures 64–70: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, p. 19, discusses the overlapping cycles in the procession: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The Sage kisses the earth
cues.text: The Sage bends to kiss the earth. Bassoons and contrabassoon play over timpani and a low bass, and the strings hold a chord.
cues.evidence: Full score, p. 74, rehearsal figure 71, Lento: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. The ballet scenario describes the Sage’s kiss: https://www.kcatalog.org/index.php/browse-chapters/kcatalog/188-k015-the-rite-of-spring.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Final dance of Part I, Prestissimo
cues.text: The bass drum starts the next dance. Winds and strings rise, and the full orchestra plays repeated figures. The marking is Prestissimo, and the dance follows the brief stillness of the Sage.
cues.evidence: Full score, pp. 74–85, rehearsal figure 72 to the end of Part I: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Introduction into the stamping chord
transitions.from: Intro · Bassoon solo in high register
transitions.how: The bassoon’s opening phrase returns and the other wind instruments drop out. Plucked violins start a short repeating figure. At Tempo giusto, second violins, violas, cellos and basses stamp the F♭ major/E♭-seventh chord, and horns mark the irregular accents.

transitions.title: Augurs to Presto, violins running
transitions.how: The heavy close of the Augurs breaks into Presto. Running violin figures and short high-wind calls cut across held horn notes, and the low strings play sharply repeated attacks.

transitions.title: Clarinets in octaves under flute trills
transitions.to: C · Spring Rounds, two clarinets, heavy dance
transitions.how: The fast dance stops. At Tranquillo, the flutes trill while E♭ clarinet and bass clarinet play in octaves; brass and strings are silent. The bass clarinet is now the lowest voice. The wind passage leads into the slower, heavy string chords of Sostenuto e pesante.

transitions.title: Round dance to low brass, Molto allegro
transitions.from: C · Spring Rounds, two clarinets, heavy dance
transitions.to: D · Ritual of the Rival Tribes
transitions.how: The round dance ends with its quiet music for flutes and clarinets. At Molto allegro the trombones and tubas enter, and the bassoons and horns reply. Low strings reinforce the tread. Within a few bars, quick high figures break across the heavy phrase.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 53–55, rehearsal figures 56–57: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, p. 19: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

transitions.title: Tuba entry before the procession heading
transitions.from: D · Ritual of the Rival Tribes
transitions.how: The tuba tune begins at figure 64, before the printed procession heading at figure 67. When the Sage arrives, the tuba is repeating its tune over bassoon and low-string figures, and the horns play a separate pattern above it. The march begins inside the crowd music. More players join, and the phrases of each part keep their own lengths.
transitions.evidence: Full score, pp. 65–73, rehearsal figures 64–70: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf. Van den Toorn, p. 19, places the tuba entrance at 64 and the procession heading at 67: https://publishing.cdlib.org/ucpressebooks/public/book/stravinsky-and-the-rite-of-spring.html

transitions.title: The procession breaks off into Lento
transitions.to: Link · The Sage kisses the earth
transitions.how: The procession breaks off and the tempo changes to Lento at figure 71. Bassoons and contrabassoon repeat their low notes over quiet timpani and a solo bass. The strings then hold a hushed chord, coloured by harmonics, before figure 72. The Sage touches the ground here.
transitions.evidence: Full score, p. 74, rehearsal figure 71 and the held chord before 72: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/a/af/IMSLP524674-PMLP179425-PMLUS00725-complete1.pdf

transitions.title: Bass-drum roll at the Prestissimo
transitions.from: Link · The Sage kisses the earth
transitions.how: The string chord is held under a pause. A bass-drum roll begins at Prestissimo, and horns and trumpets enter. An upward rush through the winds and strings follows. The bass drum continues to sound beneath the new figures.

source.title: Stravinsky, The Rite of Spring, full score, Dover reprint of corrected Boosey text
source.locator: Part I, pp. 1–85; opening and rehearsals 13, 37, 48–49, 57, 67, 71–72. Approximate passage states, not attack-level alignment. The later corrected print is used only for these shared scoring features; the different 1943 finale heard in Part II is not mapped from this score.

timeline.note: The opening centres on the high bassoon melody with sparse horn support; other reeds join as the introduction continues.
The introduction sets reed lines over sparse horn support. No string entry is identified in this excerpt.
The first Augurs block repeats a string chord; horns reinforce selected attacks. First violins are absent from this opening block.
The abduction ritual combines moving strings and short high-wind gestures with brass and percussion support.
The quiet frame of Spring Rounds places its melody in small and bass clarinets against sustained flutes.
The heavy round dance adds repeated lower-wind and string chords beneath a broad melodic line.
Low brass open the rival-tribes exchange; horn and bassoon figures answer before the higher orchestral block enters.
The procession overlaps recurring tuba and horn figures with lower strings and reeds.
Low winds and a quiet bass play under the Sage’s brief pause; a held string chord comes before the music restarts.
After the held chord, the Dance of the Earth begins with rapid sweeps and repeated massed patterns.

composer.born: 17 June 1882, Oranienbaum, near St Petersburg, Russia
composer.epithet: Composer of dance music in which a single displaced accent could unsettle the dancers, and of a psalm setting that scarcely moves.
facts: Diaghilev’s Ballets Russes · Ramuz’s travelling theatre · Balanchine · Auden and Kallman
Ballets, operas, symphonies and sacred music; composing and recording into his eighties
composer.background:
Stravinsky was born in 1882 at Oranienbaum. His father, Fyodor, sang bass at the Mariinsky Theatre in St Petersburg; Igor heard him on stage and began piano lessons at nine. He entered St Petersburg University to study law. There he befriended Vladimir Rimsky-Korsakov, whose father heard his first pieces in 1902. Rimsky-Korsakov took him on privately, giving regular lessons from 1905 until his death in 1908. The pupil orchestrated pages of Pan Voyevoda, then had to explain why his teacher had scored them differently.

He married his cousin Catherine Nossenko in 1906; by 1914 they had four children. His E♭ Symphony owed much to Glazunov and Tchaikovsky; Scherzo fantastique and Fireworks are short orchestral works. Sergei Diaghilev heard his music in 1909 and gave him some Chopin to orchestrate for Les Sylphides. A full ballet, The Firebird, followed. Stravinsky handed over the score in sections while Michel Fokine worked out the dances. In his 1936 autobiography he recalled that the rehearsals ended with dinner beside Diaghilev and Nijinsky, and good claret.
